source: In vertebrates, the total number of vertebrae is precisely defined.

source: Vertebrae derive from embryonic somites that are continuously produced posteriorly from the presomitic mesoderm (PSM) during body formation.

source: This leads to a graded repression of the Brachyury/T transcription factor, reducing mesoderm ingression and slowing down the elongation process.

claim: The continuation of somite formation while axis elongation slows leads to progressive reduction of PSM size.

source: Over-expression of Pbx1 in PM precursors after the 3-somite stage slowed down axis elongation (Figure 7L and Video 5, n = 12 embryos), suggesting that Pbx1 can restore the effect of anterior Hox genes on ingression during this time window.
evidence: This is an inference based on the Pbx1 overexpression experiment.

claim: Hox-dependent control of ingression in the paraxial mesoderm requires Pbx1 for anterior but not for posterior Hox genes.
source: Thus, Hox-dependent control of ingression in the paraxial mesoderm requires Pbx1 for anterior but not for posterior Hox genes.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the Pbx1 siRNA experiments with different Hox genes.

claim: The Wnt/βcatenin pathway targets, Axin2, Fgf8, and Sp8 were down-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells.
source: The Wnt/βcatenin pathway targets, Axin2, Fgf8, and Sp8 were down-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells (Table 1, Supplementary file 1, Figure 8B)
evidence: This is supported by microarray and qRT-PCR data shown in Table 1 and Figure 8B.

claim: Posterior Hox genes might control axis elongation rate by progressively down-regulating the Wnt/βcatenin pathway.
source: The Wnt/βcatenin pathway targets, Axin2, Fgf8, and Sp8 were down-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells (Table 1, Supplementary file 1, Figure 8B) suggesting that posterior Hox genes might control axis elongation rate by progressively down-regulating the Wnt/βcatenin pathway.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed downregulation of Wnt targets.

claim: Expression of Axin2, Fgf8, and T/Brachyury in the tail-bud is down-regulated when Hoxa13 becomes activated.
source: To test this hypothesis, we first performed in situ hybridizations (ISH) for Axin2, Fgf8, and T/Brachyury that show that their expression in the tail-bud is down-regulated when Hoxa13 becomes activated (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A–D, n = 8 embryos for each condition).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A-D.

claim: Quantitative RT-PCR on micro-dissected tail-buds shows a slight progressive down-regulation of Axin2, Fgf8, and T/Brachyury from the 10 to 20-somite stage followed by a significant decrease in gene expression at the 25-somite stage.
source: Since the ISH technique is not quantitative enough to resolve slight differences, we performed quantitative Reverse Transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) on micro-dissected tail-buds from 10, 15, 20, and 25-somite stages for Axin2, Fgf8, and T/Brachyury. These experiments show a slight progressive down-regulation of these genes from the 10 to 20-somite stage followed by a significant decrease in gene expression at the 25-somite stage correlating with the slowing down of axis elongation as well as with the timing of posterior genes expression (Figure 8C–E, n = 5 embryos for each stage).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8C-E.

claim: The decrease in Axin2, Fgf8, and T/Brachyury expression at the 25-somite stage correlates with the slowing down of axis elongation and with the timing of posterior genes expression.
source: These experiments show a slight progressive down-regulation of these genes from the 10 to 20-somite stage followed by a significant decrease in gene expression at the 25-somite stage correlating with the slowing down of axis elongation as well as with the timing of posterior genes expression (Figure 8C–E, n = 5 embryos for each stage).
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal correlation of gene expression changes with developmental events.

claim: Co-electroporation of Hoxd10, Hoxc11, or Hoxa13 with βcatLEF rescues axis elongation.
source: Co-electroporation of Hoxd10, Hoxc11, or Hoxa13 with βcatLEF (which activates the Wnt/βcatenin pathway [Galceran et al., 2001]) rescues axis elongation (Figure 8F–H, Videos 6–8, n = 41).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8F-H and Videos 6-8.

claim: Posterior Hox genes (Hoxa9, Hoxc9, Hoxd10, Hoxd11, Hoxc11, Hoxa13, Hoxb13, Hoxc13) induced a down-regulation of Wnt/βcatenin luciferase activity which increased in a collinear fashion (except for Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 which showed a weaker effect).
source: We co-electroporated a Wnt/βcatenin firefly luciferase reporter (BATLuc) and a CMV-Renilla luciferase construct in PM progenitors together with either Venus or Hoxa9, Hoxc9, Hoxd10, Hoxd11, Hoxc11, Hoxa13, Hoxb13, or Hoxc13. These Hox genes induced a down-regulation of luciferase activity which increased in a collinear fashion (except for Hoxd10 and Hoxd11 which showed a weaker effect) (Figure 8I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A, n = 83 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 8I and Figure 8—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The posterior Hox genes control axis elongation by modulating Wnt/βcatenin signaling activity.
source: All together, these results strongly suggest that the posterior Hox genes control axis elongation by modulating Wnt/βcatenin signaling activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the rescue experiments and luciferase assays.

claim: When co-expressing Hoxa9 and Hoxa13, the Wnt-repressive effect was equivalent to that of Hoxa13, indicating that posterior prevalence also applies to Wnt repression.
source: When co-expressing Hoxa9 and Hoxa13, the Wnt-repressive effect was equivalent to that of Hoxa13, indicating that posterior prevalence also applies to Wnt repression (Figure 6D–E, n = 30 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D-E.

claim: Wnt repression by Hoxa13 is independent of the quantity of protein expressed.
source: By expressing various amounts of Hoxa13, we observed that Wnt repression is independent of the quantity of protein expressed (Figure 6G–H, n = 62 embryos), suggesting that Hox proteins levels are saturating in our experiments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G-H.

claim: Hox protein levels are saturating in the overexpression experiments.
source: By expressing various amounts of Hoxa13, we observed that Wnt repression is independent of the quantity of protein expressed (Figure 6G–H, n = 62 embryos), suggesting that Hox proteins levels are saturating in our experiments.
evidence: This is an inference based on the dose-response experiment.

claim: The same posterior Hox genes can regulate ingression, axis elongation, and Wnt signaling with strikingly similar collinear trends.
source: Therefore, the same posterior Hox genes can regulate ingression, axis elongation, and Wnt signaling with strikingly similar collinear trends.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on comparing the collinear trends observed in multiple assays.

claim: Hoxa13 ingression phenotype is rescued by an activated form of Lrp6 or a stabilized form of Ctbbn1.
source: Hoxa13 ingression phenotype is rescued by an activated form of Lrp6 or a stabilized form of Ctbbn1 (Figure 8J, n = 42 embryos) but not by Wnt3a or Wnt5a (Figure 8K, n = 30 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8J.

claim: Hoxa13 ingression phenotype is not rescued by Wnt3a or Wnt5a.
source: Hoxa13 ingression phenotype is rescued by an activated form of Lrp6 or a stabilized form of Ctbbn1 (Figure 8J, n = 42 embryos) but not by Wnt3a or Wnt5a (Figure 8K, n = 30 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8K.

claim: Genetically, Hox genes act on Wnt signaling at the membrane level.
source: This suggests that, genetically, Hox genes act on Wnt signaling at the membrane level.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiments with Lrp6 and Ctbbn1.

claim: Over-expression of the Wnt receptor Fzd2 with Hoxa13 rescued Wnt repression.
source: Over-expression of the Wnt receptor Fzd2 (down-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells (Figure 8B, Table 1 and Supplementary file 1)) with Hoxa13 rescued Wnt repression (Figure 8L, n = 29 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8L.

claim: Fzd2 is expressed in the tail-bud at 15 somites and down-regulated after 25 somites.
source: Fzd2 is expressed in the tail-bud at 15 somites and down-regulated after 25 somites (Figure 8—figure supplement 1E, n = 8 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Over-expression of the Wnt pathway component Dact2 repressed Wnt activity.
source: Over-expression of the Wnt pathway component Dact2 (which is expressed in the tail-bud from 25 somites onward and up-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells [Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, n = 8 embryos, Table 1, Supplementary file 1]), repressed Wnt activity (Figure 8M, n = 9 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8M.

claim: Dact2 is expressed in the tail-bud from 25 somites onward and up-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells.
source: Over-expression of the Wnt pathway component Dact2 (which is expressed in the tail-bud from 25 somites onward and up-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells [Figure 8—figure supplement 1F, n = 8 embryos, Table 1, Supplementary file 1]), repressed Wnt activity (Figure 8M, n = 9 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by in situ hybridization and microarray data.

claim: In Hoxa13 over-expressing cells, the FGF receptor FGFR1, its ligand Fgf8, and its targets Etv1 and Cyp26A1 as well as the FGF pathway component Rasgrp3, were down-regulated while the FGF/MAPK inhibitor, Spred2, was up-regulated.
source: In Hoxa13 over-expressing cells, the FGF receptor FGFR1, its ligand Fgf8, and its targets Etv1 and Cyp26A1 as well as the FGF pathway component Rasgrp3, were down-regulated while the FGF/MAPK inhibitor, Spred2, was up-regulated (Figure 8B, Table 1, Supplementary file 1), indicating that Hoxa13 can also inhibit FGF signaling.
evidence: This is supported by microarray and qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8B and Table 1.

claim: Hoxa13 can inhibit FGF signaling.
source: In Hoxa13 over-expressing cells, the FGF receptor FGFR1, its ligand Fgf8, and its targets Etv1 and Cyp26A1 as well as the FGF pathway component Rasgrp3, were down-regulated while the FGF/MAPK inhibitor, Spred2, was up-regulated (Figure 8B, Table 1, Supplementary file 1), indicating that Hoxa13 can also inhibit FGF signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed changes in FGF pathway components.

claim: FGF inhibition by Hoxa13 is consistent with the down-regulation of PSM cell motility observed after Hoxc11 or Hoxa13 over-expression.
source: This inhibition is consistent with the down-regulation of PSM cell motility observed after Hoxc11 or Hoxa13 over-expression (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B, n = 20 embryos) (Bénazéraf et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference linking FGF inhibition to cell motility changes, supported by data and a citation.

claim: FGF and Wnt signaling reciprocally regulate each other in PM precursors.
source: FGF down-regulation is expected since FGF and Wnt signaling reciprocally regulate each other in PM precursors (Aulehla et al., 2003; Naiche et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Down-regulation of Cyp26A1 can up-regulate RA signaling leading to repression of the Wnt pathway non cell-autonomously.
source: Down-regulation of Cyp26A1, which degrades RA, can up-regulate RA signaling leading to repression of the Wnt pathway non cell-autonomously (Iulianella et al., 1999; Young et al., 2009; Martin and Kimelman, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Posterior Hox genes act on a gene network converging toward autonomous and non-autonomous negative Wnt regulation.
source: Together, these data suggest that posterior Hox genes act on a gene network converging toward autonomous and non-autonomous negative Wnt regulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the various mechanisms of Wnt regulation observed.

claim: The T-box transcription factor T (aka Brachyury) is a well-characterized Wnt target which has been shown to control cell ingression to the mesoderm.
source: The T-box transcription factor T (aka Brachyury) is a well-characterized Wnt target which has been shown to control cell ingression to the mesoderm (Wilson et al., 1995; Yamaguchi et al., 1999).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: T expression levels decrease between 10 and 20-somite stage and then significantly drop at the 25-somite stage in micro-dissected tail buds.
source: Q-PCR analysis of micro-dissected tail buds shows that T expression levels decrease between 10 and 20-somite stage and then significantly drop at the 25-somite stage (Figure 8C).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Over-expressing T by electroporation often resulted in PM-expressing cells extending more anteriorly than control cells suggesting that they ingress earlier.
source: Over-expressing T by electroporation often resulted in PM-expressing cells extending more anteriorly than control cells suggesting that they ingress earlier (Figure 9A–B, n = 6 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: Over-expression of T together with either Hoxa9, Hoxd10, Hoxc11 or Hoxa13 rescued the ingression delay.
source: Over-expression of T together with either Hoxa9, Hoxd10, Hoxc11 or Hoxa13 rescued the ingression delay (Figure 9A–B, n = 6, 11, 10 and 7 embryos respectively).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9A-B.

claim: T rescued the elongation slow down observed after Hoxa13 over-expression.
source: T also rescued the elongation slow down observed after Hoxa13 over-expression (Video 6, Figure 9C, n = 4 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Video 6 and Figure 9C.

claim: A lower dose of T (0.5 μg/μl) only led to partial rescue of the Hoxa13 phenotype.
source: A lower dose of T (0.5 μg/μl) only led to partial rescue of the Hoxa13 phenotype (Figure 9C, n = 4 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 9C.

claim: Endogenous T expression is down-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells FACS-sorted from electroporated embryos.
source: Endogenous T expression is down-regulated in Hoxa13 over-expressing cells FACS-sorted from electroporated embryos (Figure 9D, n = 2 FACS sorted cell samples for each condition).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 9D.

claim: Over-expression of Hoxc11 or Hoxa13 with a T promoter luciferase reporter shows T repression which is stronger for Hoxa13.
source: Over-expression of a reporter generated by fusing one kilobase of the chicken T promoter to the firefly luciferase (cTprLuc) together with Hoxc11 or Hoxa13 and the CMV-Renilla luciferase show T repression which is stronger for Hoxa13 (Figure 9E, n = 19 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9E.

claim: Over-expression of βcatLEF leads to T up-regulation.
source: Over-expression of βcatLEF leads to T up-regulation (Figure 9F, n = 20 embryos)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Co-expression of Hoxa13 with βcatLEF totally rescues T repression.
source: and co-expression of Hoxa13 with βcatLEF totally rescues T repression (Figure 9F, n = 20 embryos) suggesting that Hox genes down-regulate T expression by repressing the Wnt/βcatenin pathway.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9F.

claim: Hox genes down-regulate T expression by repressing the Wnt/βcatenin pathway.
source: and co-expression of Hoxa13 with βcatLEF totally rescues T repression (Figure 9F, n = 20 embryos) suggesting that Hox genes down-regulate T expression by repressing the Wnt/βcatenin pathway.
evidence: This is an inference based on the rescue experiment with βcatLEF.

claim: Over-expressing T had no effect on BATluc activation.
source: Over-expressing T had no effect on BATluc activation (Figure 9—figure supplement 1, n = 8 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The effect of Hox genes on epiblast ingression involves quantitative regulation of T expression levels.
source: This argues that the effect of Hox genes on epiblast ingression involves quantitative regulation of T expression levels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that T does not affect Wnt signaling but can rescue Hox phenotypes.

claim: A Hoxa13 truncated form is responsible for the dominant Hand-Foot-Genital syndrome in man.
source: A Hoxa13 truncated form is responsible for the dominant Hand-Foot-Genital syndrome in man (Mortlock and Innis, 1997).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A truncation in the chicken Hoxa13 homolog (Hoxa13dn) acts as a dominant-negative inhibiting the function of all Hox13 genes.
source: A similar truncation in the chicken homolog (Hoxa13dn) acts as a dominant-negative inhibiting the function of all Hox13 genes (de Santa Barbara and Roberts, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to a previous study.

claim: When over-expressed before activation of Hox13 paralogs, Hoxa13dn had no effect on BATluc activity.
source: When over-expressed before activation of Hox13 paralogs, Hoxa13dn had no effect on BATluc activity (Figure 9G, n = 18 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Co-expression of Hoxa13dn with Hoxa13 in similar conditions abolished Wnt repression.
source: However, co-expression with Hoxa13 in similar conditions abolished Wnt repression (Figure 9G, n = 18 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9G.

claim: Similar truncations in chicken Hoxd10 (Hoxd10dn) and Hoxc11 (Hoxc11dn) also exert a dominant-negative effect on their wild-type counterparts.
source: Similar truncations in chicken Hoxd10 (Hoxd10dn) and Hoxc11 ( Hoxc11dn) also exert a dominant-negative effect on their wild-type counterparts (Figure 9H–I, n = 38 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9H-I.

claim: Increasing the number of dominant-negative constructs (Hoxd10dn, Hoxc11dn, Hoxa13dn) results in a corresponding increase in luciferase activity when embryos are harvested at the 28-somite stage.
source: We over-expressed Hoxa13dn alone or combined with either Hoxc11dn or with Hoxc11dn and Hoxd10dn along with BATLuc and CMV-Renilla constructs in PM precursors of the streak at stage 8 HH. Embryos were harvested at the 28-somite stage when most Hox10-13 paralogs are expressed. Increasing the number of dominant-negative constructs results in a corresponding increase in luciferase activity (Figure 9J, n = 35 embryos).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 9J.

claim: Co-expression of the three dominant-negative vectors Hoxd10dn, Hoxc11dn, and Hoxa13dn together leads to up-regulation of T, Axin2, and Fzd2 in FACS-sorted Venus-positive cells from tail-buds of 28-somite embryos.
source: We next co-expressed the three dominant-negative vectors Hoxd10dn, Hoxc11dn, and Hoxa13dn together, along with Venus and FACS-sorted dissociated Venus-positive cells from tail-buds of 28-somite embryos. qRT-PCR analysis of T, Axin2, and Fzd2 in the Venus-positive cells shows up-regulation of the three genes (Figure 9K-L, n = 4 embryos for each condition).
evidence: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 9K-L.

claim: A subset of posterior Hox genes gradually represses Wnt/βcatenin signaling and consequently T/Brachyury in paraxial mesoderm precursors of the epiblast.
source: All together these results argue that a subset of posterior Hox genes gradually represses Wnt/βcatenin signaling and consequently T/Brachyury in paraxial mesoderm precursors of the epiblast.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the dominant-negative experiments and other data.

claim: Progressive repression of Wnt/T by posterior Hox genes leads to reduced cell ingression and cell motility in the PSM, resulting in a slowing down of axis elongation.
source: This progressive repression leads to reduced cell ingression and cell motility in the PSM, resulting in a slowing down of axis elongation.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating multiple experimental observations.

claim: Over-expression of a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa5 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ha13) does not show any repression of T luciferase activity.
source: Over-expression of cTprLuc along with a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa5 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ha13) does not show any repression of luciferase activity while over-expression of a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa13 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa5 (Hoxa13Ha5) shows a strong repression of luciferase activity (Figure 10A–B, n = 35 embryos)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: Over-expression of a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa13 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa5 (Hoxa13Ha5) shows a strong repression of T luciferase activity.
source: Over-expression of cTprLuc along with a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa5 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ha13) does not show any repression of luciferase activity while over-expression of a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa13 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa5 (Hoxa13Ha5) shows a strong repression of luciferase activity (Figure 10A–B, n = 35 embryos)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 10A-B.

claim: The homeodomain does not contain the major domain responsible for T/Brachyury repression by posterior Hox genes.
source: Over-expression of cTprLuc along with a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa5 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ha13) does not show any repression of luciferase activity while over-expression of a chimera where the homeodomain of Hoxa13 has been swapped with the one from Hoxa5 (Hoxa13Ha5) shows a strong repression of luciferase activity (Figure 10A–B, n = 35 embryos) suggesting that the homeodomain does not contain the major domain responsible for T/Brachyury repression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chimera experiments.

claim: Overexpression of a chimera where the N-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the N-ter of Hoxa13 (NHoxa13HCa5) shows a strong repression of T luciferase activity.
source: Overexpression of a chimera where the N-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the N-ter of Hoxa13 (NHoxa13HCa5) shows a strong repression of luciferase activity while a chimera where the C-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the C-ter of Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ca13) does not show any repression (Figure 10C–D, n = 16 embryos)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 10C-D.

claim: A chimera where the C-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the C-ter of Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ca13) does not show any repression of T luciferase activity.
source: Overexpression of a chimera where the N-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the N-ter of Hoxa13 (NHoxa13HCa5) shows a strong repression of luciferase activity while a chimera where the C-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the C-ter of Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ca13) does not show any repression (Figure 10C–D, n = 16 embryos)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 10C-D.

claim: The N-ter region of Hoxa13 contains the domain responsible for the repression of T/Brachyury.
source: Overexpression of a chimera where the N-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the N-ter of Hoxa13 (NHoxa13HCa5) shows a strong repression of luciferase activity while a chimera where the C-ter of Hoxa5 is swapped with the C-ter of Hoxa13 (Hoxa5Ca13) does not show any repression (Figure 10C–D, n = 16 embryos) suggesting that the N-ter region of Hoxa13 contains the domain responsible for the repression of T/Brachyury.
evidence: This is an inference based on the chimera experiments.

claim: Sequence alignment of the N-terminal regions of Hoxa9, d10, c11, and a13 shows little conservation at the amino acid level.
source: Sequence alignment of the N-terminal regions of Hoxa9, d10, c11, and a13 shows little conservation at the amino acid level suggesting that it is not a conserved amino acid domain but rather a structural domain that is responsible for the repression activity of these proteins (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 10—figure supplement 1.

claim: It is not a conserved amino acid domain but rather a structural domain that is responsible for the repression activity of posterior Hox proteins.
source: Sequence alignment of the N-terminal regions of Hoxa9, d10, c11, and a13 shows little conservation at the amino acid level suggesting that it is not a conserved amino acid domain but rather a structural domain that is responsible for the repression activity of these proteins (Figure 10—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the lack of sequence conservation.

claim: When overexpressing Hoxc11Ha5 or Hoxa13Ha5, a stronger down-regulation of T/Brachyury is observed with the chimera containing the Hoxc11 N-ter than with the one containing the Hoxa13 N-ter.
source: Surprisingly, when we overexpress Hoxc11Ha5 or Hoxa13Ha5 along with cTprLuc, we observe a stronger down-regulation of T/Brachyury with the chimera containing the Hoxc11 N-ter than with the one containing the Hoxa13 N-ter (Figure 10E–F, n = 26 embryos)
evidence: This is supported by luciferase assay data shown in Figure 10E-F.

claim: The homeodomain could be responsible for fine tuning T/Brachyury repression by posterior Hox genes.
source: Surprisingly, when we overexpress Hoxc11Ha5 or Hoxa13Ha5 along with cTprLuc, we observe a stronger down-regulation of T/Brachyury with the chimera containing the Hoxc11 N-ter than with the one containing the Hoxa13 N-ter (Figure 10E–F, n = 26 embryos) suggesting that the homeodomain could be responsible for fine tuning T/Brachyury repression.
evidence: This is an inference based on the unexpected result from the chimera experiments.

claim: The progressive deployment of posterior Hox genes in PM precursors during axis elongation leads to a collinear repression of the Wnt/βcatenin pathway and its target T/Brachyury.
source: Altogether our data suggest that the progressive deployment of posterior Hox genes in PM precursors during axis elongation leads to a collinear repression of the Wnt/βcatenin pathway and its target T/Brachyury.
evidence: This is a conclusion integrating all the experimental findings.

claim: A subset of posterior Hox genes represses Wnt/T signaling with increasing strength showing a collinear trend.
source: Here, we show that a subset of posterior Hox genes represses Wnt/T signaling with increasing strength showing a collinear trend.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by multiple experiments.

claim: A similar collinear effect of posterior genes overexpressed in PM precursors is observed on delaying their ingression in the PSM and on the slowing down of axis elongation.
source: We observe a similar collinear effect of these posterior genes overexpressed in PM precursors on delaying their ingression in the PSM and on the slowing down of axis elongation.
evidence: This is a summary of findings supported by the consecutive electroporation and elongation experiments.

claim: Inhibition of Wnt signaling by posterior Hox genes is accompanied by a down-regulation of FGF signaling which was shown to control elongation velocity by regulating cell motility in the PSM.
source: This inhibition of Wnt signaling is accompanied by a down-regulation of FGF signaling which was shown to control elongation velocity by regulating cell motility in the PSM (Bénazéraf et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by the microarray data and a citation.

claim: Posterior Hox genes are involved in the slowing down of axis elongation by acting both on the flux of cells in the posterior PSM and on the motility of PSM cells.
source: This suggests that posterior Hox genes are involved in the slowing down of axis elongation by acting both on the flux of cells in the posterior PSM and on the motility of PSM cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed effects on ingression and cell motility.

claim: In the chicken embryo, PM precursors originate initially from the lateral epiblast which migrate toward the midline during formation of the primitive streak.
source: In the chicken embryo, PM precursors originate initially from the lateral epiblast which migrate toward the midline during formation of the primitive streak ( Selleck and Stern, 1991; Hatada and Stern, 1994).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Around stage 4 HH, somite precursors begin to ingress from the superficial epiblast of the anterior primitive streak and posterior Node region.
source: Around stage 4 HH, somite precursors begin to ingress from the superficial epiblast of the anterior primitive streak and posterior Node region (Psychoyos and Stern, 1996; Iimura et al., 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Two types of PM precursors have been identified in chicken and mouse embryos.
source: Two types of PM precursors have been identified in chicken and mouse embryos (Wilson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: A first set of PM precursors derives from the Node/primitive streak border and exhibits long-term self-renewal properties.
source: A first set derives from the Node/primitive streak border and exhibits long-term self-renewal properties (Selleck and Stern, 1991; Cambray and Wilson, 2002, 2007).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: The first set of PM precursors express Sox2 and Brachyury and they can contribute both to the PM (mostly to the medial part of the somites) and to the neural tube.
source: These cells express Sox2 and Brachyury and they can contribute both to the PM (mostly to the medial part of the somites) and to the neural tube (Ordahl, 1993; McGrew et al., 2008; Tzouanacou et al., 2009; Kondoh and Takemoto, 2012; Olivera-Martinez et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: A second set of PM precursors derives from the anterior portion of the primitive streak and contributes to shorter clones restricted to the PM.
source: A second set derives from the anterior portion of the primitive streak and contributes to shorter clones restricted to the PM (Iimura et al., 2007; McGrew et al., 2008; Tzouanacou et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: After stage 4 HH, in the chicken embryo, the primitive streak begins to regress and after stage 13-14 HH, it becomes part of the tail-bud.
source: After stage 4 HH, in the chicken embryo, the primitive streak begins to regress and after stage 13-14 HH, it becomes part of the tail-bud (Schoenwolf, 1979).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by a citation.

claim: At the 25-somite stage (stage 15 HH), the posterior neuropore closes and the tail-bud becomes enclosed into the tail fold.
source: At the 25-somite stage (stage 15 HH), the posterior neuropore closes and the tail-bud becomes enclosed into the tail fold.
evidence: This is established knowledge about chicken embryo development.

claim: During stages 4-15 HH, PM precursors are continuously produced first by the primitive streak and then by the tail-bud.
source: During these stages, PM precursors are continuously produced first by the primitive streak and then by the tail-bud.
